$comment: Target profile for a moisture-loving nitrophile. Nettle follows water and disturbed, enriched ground - stream banks, avalanche tracks, road edges, old farmyards - so habitat_model 'riparian' is the right signal, with a wide distance band because it tolerates drier ground than devil's club does.
habitat_note: Stream banks, seepage lines, avalanche runouts, damp thickets and enriched disturbed ground, from valley bottom to lower subalpine. Wants moisture and nitrogen, and follows people: many of the best patches in this region are old homesteads and road edges. Scored on two signals - the vegetation layer for the open, lush, disturbed ground it occupies, and the moisture component for the damp part of it - with a wide moisture band because nettle will take a drier site if the soil is rich.

weights_override.$comment: A two-signal species: the vegetation layer finds the open, green, disturbed ground it wants and the moisture component finds the damp part of it. Aspect is zero-weighted - for a plant following water and disturbance, which way the ground faces is not the binding variable.

folk_magic.$comment: European magical use is unusually strong for a plant this common, and it is worth separating from the Indigenous food-and-fibre use, which is a different kind of record.
traditions: British Isles and European folk magic
Indigenous North American nations (food, fibre and medicine)

associations.note: Nettle was a protective plant: carried in a pouch, strewn in the home, or grown by the door to keep harm and ill-wishing out. In the British Isles a bundle of nettle was thrown on the fire to avert lightning and to turn aside evil, and it was one of the herbs a household was expected to have to hand for that purpose.
associations.origin: British Isles and wider European folk practice; the lightning and warding uses are standard in the folk-herb record.

associations.note: Used to drive out evil and break curses, thrown after an ill-wisher or into a room to clear it, and in some accounts used to return a curse to its sender. The plant's sting is part of the logic - it was a herb that fought back.
associations.origin: European folk magic; the banishing and curse-returning uses are recorded in the British and German folk record.

associations.note: Nettle burned or hung to turn away lightning and storms, a use shared with several of the protective herbs in this set. It belongs with the warding uses above rather than standing on its own.
associations.origin: European folk tradition, most strongly attested in the British Isles.

associations.note: Nettle's other long record is medicinal and dietary: a spring tonic and cooked green, a fibre plant whose stems were retted and spun into cloth, and - most oddly - urtication, the deliberate stinging of a joint to treat arthritic pain, which is a real and repeatedly documented practice rather than a joke.
associations.origin: European herbalism for the tonic, textile and urtication traditions; Indigenous North American nations used nettle for food, cordage and medicine in closely comparable ways.

safety.note: The stinging hairs are the obvious hazard and cause a rash in most people. Cooked or blanched, the plant is a safe and ordinary green - the sting is destroyed by heat and drying. As a medicine it is a diuretic and may interact with blood thinners, blood-pressure and diabetes medication, and it is traditionally avoided in pregnancy because it can stimulate the uterus. Do not attempt urtication without knowing what you are doing. This note is a hazard summary, not a dosage.

sources: Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (17th c.) - European medicinal and protective use.
British and German folk-magic compilations for the warding, banishing and lightning uses.
Turner, N. J., and Moerman, D. - Indigenous North American food, fibre and medicinal use.

observations.$comment: 13 research-grade records in the AOI, and iNaturalist's Urtica dioica is a species complex (the native U. dioica subsp. gracilis plus the introduced subspecies), which is fine here - all of them want the same damp enriched ground.

elevation_m.$comment: Valley bottom through the lower slopes; it thins out as the growing season shortens and the ground gets poorer.

aspect.$comment: Unused (subweight 0). Kept because the terrain stage reads it.

vegetation.$comment: Scored as open, lush, disturbed ground. Nettle is a nitrophile: it wants full light and enriched soil, which in this landscape means the greenest, most productive ground rather than the thin sward the dry-site species occupy.

logging.$comment: Nettle follows disturbance, so the penalty is light and fades quickly - a fresh landing or a new road edge is genuine nettle ground.

moisture.$comment: The damp half of the plant's requirement, and a preference rather than a hard requirement - nettle will take a dry site if the soil is enriched, which is what the min_credit floor says. The topographic-position term matters as much as the water distance here: nettle follows ditches, old farmyards and seepage lines that are often unmapped.
